Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

(CNN) -- In a new anti-Israel, anti-U.S. video, an American al Qaeda member makes reference to his Jewish ancestry for the first time in an official al Qaeda message. Adam Yahiye Gadahn, also known as Azzam the American, is seen in an earlier al Qaeda video. In the video, Adam Yahiye Gadahn, also known as Azzam the American, discusses his roots as he castigates U.S. policies and deplores Israel's offensive in Gaza that started in late December 2008 and continued into January. "Let me here tell you something about myself and my biography, in which there is a benefit and a lesson," Gadahn says, as he elicits support from his fellow Muslims for "our weapons, funds and Jihad against the Jews and their allies everywhere." "Your speaker has Jews in his ancestry, the last of whom was his grandfather," he says. Growing up in rural California, Gadahn embraced Islam in the mid-1990s, moved to Pakistan and has appeared in al Qaeda videos before. He was indicted in the United States in 2006 on charges of treason and material support to al Qaeda, according to the FBI. Gadahn is on the FBI's Most Wanted List, with a reward of up to $1 million leading to his capture. FBI records show Gadahn's date of birth as September 1, 1978. The video -- in which Gadahn speaks Arabic, with English subtitles -- surfaced on Saturday. This account is based on an English transcript provided by As-Sahab Media, the media production company used by al Qaeda. Gadahn's Jewish ancestry has been reported in the news media. But terrorism analyst Laura Mansfield says it is the first time Gadahn acknowledged his Jewish ancestry in an official al Qaeda message. Gadahn says his grandfather was a "Zionist" and "a zealous supporter of the usurper entity, and a prominent member of a number of Zionist hate organizations." "He used to repeat to me what he claimed are the virtues of this entity and encouraged me to visit it, specifically the city of Tel Aviv, where relatives of ours live," says Gadahn, referring to Israel. He says his grandfather gave him a book by Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called "A Place Among the Nations" -- in which the "rabid Zionist" sets out "feeble arguments and unmasked lies to justify the Jews' rape of Muslim Palestine." But Gadahn says that despite his youth at the time, he didn't heed his grandfather's words. "How can a person with an ounce of self-respect possibly stand in the ranks of criminals and killers who have no morals, no mercy, no humanity and indeed, no honor?" he says in reference to Zionists and Israel. "Isn't it shameful enough for a person to carry the citizenship of America, the symbol of oppression and tyranny and advocate of terror in the world?" Mansfield thinks the video may have been made between late April and mid-May, before President Obama's speech in Cairo, Egypt, addressing U.S. relations with Muslims. Gadahn notes Obama's inauguration, Netanyahu's election in February, and Obama's speech in Turkey in April. Specifically mentioning the Gaza offensive and citing other hot spots such as Iraq, Afghanistan, Chechnya and Somalia, where the "Zio-Crusader alliance" is fighting his "brothers," he says "this open-faced aggression" comes as Obama has risen to power. He scorns Obama's statements in his inaugural address and in Turkey that America isn't and won't be at war with Islam, and "other deceptive, false and sugarcoated words of endearment and respect." He says Obama's language is similar to words Netanyahu uttered in the Knesset in 1996. Gadahn also backs the idea of targeting "Zio-Crusader" interests anywhere in the world, not just "within Palestine."

Gadahn says that, despite his youth at the time, he did not heed his grandfather’s words.

“How can a person with an ounce of self-respect possibly stand in the ranks of criminals and killers who have no morals, no mercy, no humanity and indeed, no honor?” he says, referring to Zionists and Israel.

“Isn’t it shameful enough for a person to carry the citizenship of America, the symbol of oppression and tyranny and advocate of terror in the world?”

(CNN) — In a newly released video attacking Israel and the United States, American al Qaeda member Adam Yahiye Gadahn publicly refers to his Jewish family background for the first time in an official message from the organization.

Gadahn, also called “Azzam the American” and previously shown in other al Qaeda recordings, speaks about his ancestry while condemning U.S. policy and Israel’s military operation in Gaza, which began in late December 2008 and continued into January. Appealing to fellow Muslims to support armed jihad against Jews and their allies with weapons and money, he says there is a lesson to be learned from his personal history.

Gadahn states that he has Jewish ancestors, the most recent being his grandfather. Raised in rural California, he converted to Islam during the mid-1990s, later relocated to Pakistan and has appeared in several earlier al Qaeda videos.

According to the FBI, U.S. authorities indicted him in 2006 on treason charges and for allegedly providing material support to al Qaeda. He is included on the FBI’s Most Wanted List, and authorities have offered as much as $1 million for information resulting in his capture. FBI files give his birth date as September 1, 1978.

The Arabic-language recording, which includes English subtitles, emerged on Saturday. This report relies on an English transcript issued by As-Sahab Media, al Qaeda’s media-production organization.

Although news outlets had previously reported Gadahn’s Jewish heritage, terrorism analyst Laura Mansfield said this was the first official al Qaeda statement in which he personally acknowledged it.

In the video, Gadahn characterizes his grandfather as a Zionist, a committed supporter of Israel and an important participant in several organizations Gadahn describes as Zionist hate groups. He says his grandfather often spoke to him about what he considered Israel’s virtues and urged him to travel there—particularly to Tel Aviv, where members of their extended family lived.

Gadahn also says his grandfather gave him Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s book *A Place Among the Nations*. He denounces Netanyahu as an extreme Zionist and claims the book uses weak reasoning and obvious falsehoods to defend what Gadahn calls the Jewish seizure of Muslim Palestine.

Despite being young at the time, Gadahn says he rejected his grandfather’s arguments. Referring to Zionists and Israel, he asks how anyone with self-respect could align with people he portrays as immoral and merciless criminals and killers. He also says that merely possessing U.S. citizenship is disgraceful, describing America as a global emblem of oppression, tyranny and support for terrorism.

Mansfield estimates that the recording was probably produced sometime from late April to mid-May, before President Barack Obama delivered his Cairo address on U.S. relations with Muslims. In his remarks, Gadahn refers to Obama’s inauguration, Netanyahu’s election in February and Obama’s April speech in Turkey.

Citing the Gaza operation as well as conflicts in Iraq, Afghanistan, Chechnya and Somalia—places where he says a “Zio-Crusader alliance” is battling his fellow Muslims—Gadahn argues that this overt aggression has continued since Obama took office.

He dismisses Obama’s statements in his inaugural address and in Turkey that the United States was not, and would not be, at war with Islam. Gadahn labels those remarks and other expressions of respect and goodwill as dishonest, misleading and deliberately softened. He further claims that Obama’s rhetoric resembles language Netanyahu used before the Knesset in 1996.

Gadahn also endorses attacks on what he calls “Zio-Crusader” interests throughout the world rather than limiting such actions to Palestinian territory.

An American-born al Qaeda member has acknowledged that he has Jewish ancestry while delivering a sharply anti-Israel and anti-U.S. message in a newly released propaganda video.

Adam Yahiye Gadahn said his grandfather was Jewish but rejected any suggestion that the family connection affected his extremist views. In the recording, Gadahn denounced Israel and repeated al Qaeda accusations against the United States, using inflammatory language aimed at Jewish people and Western governments.

The video appeared on extremist websites and was circulated by organizations that monitor militant communications. Its authenticity could not immediately be independently verified.

Gadahn, who grew up in California and converted to Islam as a teenager, became one of al Qaeda’s most prominent English-language propagandists. U.S. authorities charged him with treason in 2006, accusing him of providing aid and comfort to the terrorist organization.

His comments about his ancestry appeared intended to preempt criticism over his family background while reinforcing al Qaeda’s broader propaganda campaign. The video offered no evidence for its allegations and echoed rhetoric long used by the group to recruit followers and justify violence.

U.S. officials have repeatedly warned that al Qaeda videos are designed to attract publicity, spread disinformation and encourage attacks.

Adam Gadahn, a California native who converted to Islam and became one of al Qaeda’s most prominent English-language propagandists, invoked his family background while denouncing Israel and appealing to Muslims to support violence against it and its allies.

In the recording, distributed through extremist media channels, Gadahn acknowledged that his grandfather was Jewish. News organizations are withholding specific passages that could serve to amplify the group’s incitement.

The message’s authenticity could not immediately be independently verified. U.S. officials had no immediate public comment.

Born Adam Pearlman, Gadahn grew up in Southern California and later adopted the name Azzam al-Amriki, or “Azzam the American.” He has appeared in multiple al Qaeda videos and was indicted in the United States on treason and terrorism-related charges.

His reference to his ancestry marks a notable shift in his public rhetoric. Although Gadahn’s family history has previously been reported, he had not been known to discuss it directly in al Qaeda propaganda.

The latest message appears intended both to attract international attention and to portray al Qaeda as a leading force in the campaign against Israel and Western governments. Counterterrorism analysts caution that such releases are designed to provoke, recruit and generate publicity, even when they provide no evidence of a specific or imminent plot.
